3b17489797b345994e3d7768.title_original: When the Approved File Is Unchanged: Authority-Set Integrity for Deployment and Coding-Agent Approvals
3b17489797b345994e3d7768.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An approval for a deployment, a release, or an agent-issued command is recorded against one object: a workflow file, a script, a command line. The run that follows also reads other repository files, which decide what the deployment creates and which changes a policy allows, so an edit to one of them after approval passes any check on the approved object. Such edits are the common case. In the history of 20 public repositories, 296 of the 542 commits that change a file the run reads (54.6%) leave the approved file untouched, all of them ordinary development with no adversary involved. We demonstrate the consequence on two of those repositories: an edit outside the approved workflow adds a bucket-write policy to a deployed role, a one-line edit removes the human approval required for high-risk changes, and a check on the approved file accepts both. We define authority-set integrity: an approval is sound when it binds every repository file the authorized run is configured to read, and exact when it binds no other file. A binding over that set rejects both edits and re-requests a standing approval on about one commit in ten. The hard part is naming the set. Coding agents asked to produce the binding compute the digest correctly and bind different file sets from run to run, so a checker cannot take the set on the agent's word. It should compute the digest itself and draw the set from a source it can verify, such as the deployment too

8c0f52f9075a5b0822d61844.title_original: The Agent Clicks Approve: Injected Page Text Makes Browser Agents Authorize Access the Task Never Named
8c0f52f9075a5b0822d61844.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A browser agent that works in its user's signed-in session can be steered by a two-sentence note on a page it reads into approving a third party's access to the user's account. The agent is a confused deputy: the session supplies the authority, the page designates the access request to approve or the webhook URL to register, and nothing at the point of action checks one against the other. The agent thereby supplies the approval click that a consent screen reserves for the account holder. We measure this failure on two authorization surfaces, an OAuth-style access grant and a webhook registration, with agents built on an open-source browser framework and models from two providers. Without a defense the unauthorized action completed in all 73 attack runs. An instruction telling the model that only the user's task authorizes a grant still left 7 of 10 consent attacks completing. We therefore move the check to where the action completes. The authority envelope gate has the service accept a request only when it matches the task's envelope, the client and account or the webhook URL that the user's task named, fixed before the agent starts. With the gate the agent still sent the request in every one of 70 attack runs, the service rejected each, and the action completed in every control run whose task named it. A service that receives the task's envelope should therefore check agent-driven authorization requests against it.

6d0ce6a0f7180d7357aa81c3.title_original: On the Effectiveness of NetFlow-Based Deanonymization of Tor Onion Services (Extended Version)
6d0ce6a0f7180d7357aa81c3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the context of Tor, deanonymization attacks via traffic correlation have long been studied for both clients and onion services. We then introduce a stronger active attack based on controlled introduction requests, which removes application-specific assumptions and gives adversaries more flexibility while achieving comparable success rates. Finally, we present a passive deanonymization attack that sends zero traffic to target onion services. The attack exploits Tor's puzzle-based DoS defense as a side channel: public puzzle difficulty reveals service-load changes that can be semantically matched against NetFlow traces. 100d5495c4d24ffb3810282f.title_original: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
100d5495c4d24ffb3810282f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.

651270d9af167002db6b9137.title_original: Training-Data Extraction from Genomic Language Models
651270d9af167002db6b9137.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, exposing a direct route for studying training-sequence extraction through the generation interface. We present an output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 that selects convergent groups of repeated generations without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access during candidate selection. Recovered content is then scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Across 304 runs on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes, the attack yields 888 candidate clusters, of which 85 match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a cluster-level attack success rate of 9.57%. Final filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at the 500-bp threshold and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training-sequence regions, respectively. Within-category source-homology screening retains 11 of the 22 events at a 99% exclusion threshold and four at 98%, with the latter mapping to two reference regions. The results establish convergence among repeated nucleotide generations as a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments and characterize how recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.

7c93b4950dd7bc6a2cb28286.title_original: From Observations to Authorized Actions: Measuring Source Information in Android Agents
7c93b4950dd7bc6a2cb28286.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Android agents read content from applications and web pages and act on it with the user's authority, yet they cannot reliably tell where that content came from -- its source, the application or document that supplied it. Our application-source monitor withholds side-effecting calls whose signed source record contains an untrusted application. With the source set derived from the OS accessibility log, it blocked every selected attack write in the tested runs, but it also withheld benign sends issued after reading untrusted content, flagged benign tasks that use external content, and carried source records into a later clean task. Our WebView source-reference gate uses records from a modified browser to check object origins and reference lifetime through direct calls; in a separate 24-trial evaluation, the live agent selected no disallowed object. 8cb1fd30e608fdbc6993dd72.title_original: Poisoned into Action: Context Attacks on Typed Decision Workflows
8cb1fd30e608fdbc6993dd72.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision interfaces restrict models to predefined actions, yet schema-valid choices can still trigger policy-violating state changes. Evaluating context poisoning thus requires connecting model decisions to execution outcomes while accounting for legitimate automation retained by defenses. We introduce an execution-aware protocol tracing poisoned evidence through retrieval, model choice, automated action, and persisted state. We evaluate it with 1,659 fresh calls to Jev-1.13.0 across 20 development tasks in two synthetic workflows, using three repetitions per condition. Under natural retrieval, a standalone payload reaches all 60 trials and produces five security-violating executions, while a carrier-payload pair exposes the payload in 57 trials and produces one violation. An initial source-exclusion gate blocks the pair's observed violation but also withholds ten otherwise correct attacked decisions and sixteen correct clean decisions. Correcting its empty-scope behavior restores twelve clean decisions without additional model calls. Factorial controls show that adding correct evidence reduces wrong executions from 119/120 to 55/120 in the semantic arm and from 60/120 to zero in the neutral arm, suggesting that much of the improvement reflects general evidence value rather than attack-specific protection. Three prespecified contrasts are not statistically supported after Holm correction, so the findings remain exploratory

9ae418c7cb6d4868035fae90.title_original: Fetch Me If You Can: A Comprehensive Analysis of Fetch Metadata
9ae418c7cb6d4868035fae90.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective server-side defenses against cross-site attacks depend on understanding the context in which browser requests are generated. However, servers often lack the information needed to distinguish legitimate requests from potentially malicious cross-site interactions. Fetch Metadata, a security mechanism introduced in 2019, addresses this limitation by adding a set of HTTP headers to outgoing browser requests. These headers provide servers with information about a request's context and provenance, enabling them to enforce request isolation policies accordingly. However, the extent of Fetch Metadata's real-world adoption and its interaction with existing security mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we present the first large-scale measurement study of Fetch Metadata adoption. We analyze the top 1M websites in the Tranco list to detect deployments of Fetch Metadata isolation policies and identify custom policies used in the wild. We then examine how these policies address cross-site threats and assess their security coverage. Finally, we provide the first systematic comparison of Fetch Metadata with existing client-side security mechanisms, revealing security gaps that arise from differences between client-side and server-side enforcement.

4bc66acc10d266a698e09c17.title_original: Riemannian Suppression of Cross-Session Identity Leakage in Motor-Imagery EEG
4bc66acc10d266a698e09c17.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) recorded for motor-imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) carries subject-identifying structure that persists across sessions, allowing separately released sessions from the same person to be linked. Across two public datasets and five attackers spanning four covariance-space representations, the worst attacker falls from 90.8% to 15.6% on BCI Competition IV-2a and from 90.8% to 9.9% on OpenBMI, at a cost of 7.0 and 2.1 points of MI decoding accuracy relative to the 8-30 Hz input, and no aggregation rule exceeds chance by more than two points at any batch size. 89c5c331a2a1f43ce681c513.title_original: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
89c5c331a2a1f43ce681c513.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. 5a166c9e8249e4b55eb8aedf.title_original: Privacy Conductor: An Architectural Enforcement of Contextual Integrity in LLM-Based Document Retrieval
5a166c9e8249e4b55eb8aedf.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) that retrieve internal documents within an organization must decide who may receive them. 6277505b3cb23c417877dee4.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past decade, Metaverse technology (AR/VR) has seen widespread adoption in numerous areas, including gaming, social networking, and online collaboration. 7c5bdbdf58a2cc8285101843.title_original: Forensic Text Recovery from Document Thumbnails Using Text-Aware U-Net
7c5bdbdf58a2cc8285101843.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forensic analysis of low-resolution Word thumbnails presents a significant challenge because these artifacts may constitute the only remaining visual evidence of deleted documents. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the NLD, enabling reliable recovery of machine-readable text from severely degraded thumbnails.

a043710f177b09934185edaf.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Authorization checks at individual tool calls do not reveal how long earlier authority remains usable. 4fb1769249336701cd8fd7ba.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: \textbf{(Context)} LLM agents increasingly delegate subtasks while holding authority over sensitive data, creating confused-deputy risks: an injected delegate can exfiltrate data, amplify its authority, or act after revocation. 5013060f17acdb6f880c7617.title_original: Adversarial Robustness of Camera-Radar Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Driving
5013060f17acdb6f880c7617.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous driving (AD) relies on multi-sensor perception to interpret the surrounding environment. 5c4ed23990a668969f76de3d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Confidential Error-correcting Codes (CECs), a new cryptographic primitive that enables reliable decoding from perturbed codewords while preserving message confidentiality. 900841249178d2873a77fc20.title_original: HDKEM: Authentication Allocation for Deniable Hybrid Key Exchange
900841249178d2873a77fc20.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deniable authenticated key exchange (DAKE) establishes a shared key without leaving transferable evidence that a party participated. HDKEM binds all public session values, including a QKD key identifier when present, into authentication and key derivation. a97eb40a64b49a829c3d3d0c.title_original: ML-Assisted Power Side-Channel Attacks on ML Accelerators in Shared FPGAs
a97eb40a64b49a829c3d3d0c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud providers offer on-demand access to Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), and multi-tenant FPGAs let multiple users share one device to improve utilization. This sharing introduces security risks: an adversary co-located with a victim on the same FPGA can mount power side-channel attacks against the victim's Machine Learning (ML) accelerator. Prior on-chip attacks on such accelerators based on Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) sensors have recovered only small, MNIST-scale grayscale inputs, including with ML-assisted reconstruction. This work is the first on-chip, TDC-based attack to produce full-scale color reconstructions of ImageNet-scale inputs, by combining ML-based upscaling and recoloring with TDC measurements of a remote victim's ML accelerator. We frame this as a proof-of-concept leakage study: the victim implements the first convolution layer of a CNN processing 224x224 ImageNet inputs on a shared FPGA, which we isolate to characterize the input-dependent leakage, and we quantify how much of each reconstruction reflects genuinely recovered information versus ML-generated post-processing. As a preliminary countermeasure, we study a pixel-substitution defense that replaces each pixel value, within a fixed intensity budget, with one of different Hamming Weight, producing a different TDC signature. We find that this transformation costs the victim's own model more accuracy than it costs the attacker and, because it a

61a60ad794c09aaf93d49a48.title_original: ATTCK-R: Knowledge-Aware Long-Horizon Jailbreaking for Protected LLMs
61a60ad794c09aaf93d49a48.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models are deployed behind increasingly sophisticated safety mechanisms, evaluating their robustness under realistic adversarial conditions becomes increasingly difficult and critical. Existing jailbreaking evaluations often rely on static prompts, limited interaction horizons, or lightly protected systems, failing to reflect protected deployment settings with prompt-based safety protections. We show that the introduction of a prompt-based safety protection reduces the average attack success rate of a strong multi-turn baseline from 0.896 to 0.608 (32.1\% relative), demonstrating that unprotected evaluations substantially overestimate real-world vulnerabilities. We propose Adaptive Traceback and Tactic Curation for Knowledge-based Red-teaming (ATTCK-R), a planning-driven multi-turn red teaming framework designed for protected black-box systems. ATTCK-R models jailbreaking as a long-horizon trajectory optimization problem using a structured belief state, introduces optimization-based tactic curation to abstract reusable strategies from prior successes and failures, and employs informed traceback to resume attacks from strategically meaningful states rather than restarting. Evaluated across 9 widely used LLMs configured with a single prompt-based safety protection layer, ATTCK-R consistently outperforms strong recent multi-turn jailbreaking frameworks. Ablation results confirm that long-horizon planning and tacti

f8f79a55a9c96f22cf9d6fdf.title_original: Doctor Trigger: A Framework for Release-Bound Face Verification
f8f79a55a9c96f22cf9d6fdf.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Face swapping and generative editing enable realistic facial manipulation, while online redistribution complicates publisher oversight of circulating face images. Existing approaches establish provenance, detect manipulation, recover embedded watermarks, verify image integrity, or disrupt unauthorized face manipulation. These capabilities do not necessarily establish consistency with a specific publisher-enrolled release, limiting the evidence available for verification and human review. To address this gap, we introduce Doctor Trigger, a framework for verifying circulating faces against private publisher-held release records. Before publication, the publisher embeds a weak keyed Fourier-phase signal in each face while preserving visual fidelity and stores its spectral reference. Afterward, verification compares the circulating face with that reference and uses key projection to measure retention of the release-specific signal. Therefore, relation and key evidence jointly help publishers identify suspicious copies for review, potentially reducing the circulation of manipulated images. Experimental results across FF++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF show that spectral agreement separates tested face swaps and generative manipulations from enrolled releases, while the keyed signal distinguishes published versions from their unreleased originals under the evaluated key-preserving benign transformations. Doctor Trigger complements provenance me

eee57eb6b54b2d8cd8eb2e7a.title_original: Resource-constrained Remote Attestation of Smart Meters Using Merkle Trees in a Trusted Execution Environment
eee57eb6b54b2d8cd8eb2e7a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart meters are pivotal to the functioning of smart grids, as they measure and transmit energy consumption data that includes sensitive information about household energy usage patterns. While this data offers significant financial benefits, it can also reveal detailed insights into residents' daily routines, making the security of smart meters a critical concern. This paper introduces a novel remote attestation method for smart meters that ensures the integrity and privacy of data exchanged between smart meters and central servers while detecting unauthorized tampering. Our approach structures the communication data into a Merkle Tree-a hash data structure that facilitates efficient data integrity and authenticity verification. All operations involved in constructing the Merkle root and hashing critical data are executed in the secure environment of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) using OP-TEE, thereby maintaining the integrity and security of the smart meter's data. Comparing our experimental results with the related works highlights the superiority of our method in terms of resource efficiency, security robustness, and the feasibility of implementation on smart meters and resource-constrained devices, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of smart grid systems.

85a5cc10fbeb7fd8d1bafd4d.title_original: Risk-aware Road-network Trajectory Synthesis under Local Differential Privacy
85a5cc10fbeb7fd8d1bafd4d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Road-network trajectory synthesis under local differential privacy (LDP) enables mobility data analysis without uploading raw trajectories to an untrusted server. Existing locally private trajectory synthesis methods mainly model whole trajectories, point sequences, or grid-level mobility patterns. However, they cannot handle non-uniform privacy risks caused by local road-network and trajectory contexts, such as endpoints, long-stay-associated regions, and low-out-degree branches. They also do not directly protect conditional next-hop choices on road networks, where a user's selected successor may reveal sensitive local movement intentions. To address these challenges, we propose TrajRACE, a locally private synthesis framework for road-network trajectories. TrajRACE uses start, segment-count, and transition reports to represent trajectories. For each transition, it keeps the current road segment as a public aggregation context and perturbs the true successor among legal successors on the client side. It then assigns risk-aware protection strengths to transitions according to local road-network and trajectory contexts. Finally, the server recovers population-level start, segment-count, and conditional transition statistics from heterogeneous privatized reports, and generates synthetic trajectories that follow the public road-network topology. Experiments on three road-network trajectory datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of T

c98d71eb763d269e51bbf237.title_original: Purpose IR: Compiling User Purpose for Privacy-Preserving Agent Workflow State
c98d71eb763d269e51bbf237.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-agent workflows routinely transform rich observations into plans, summaries, memories, handoffs, and other reusable state. This creates a privacy boundary that task relevance alone does not capture: an observation may be needed as evidence for a task without its full semantics being authorized to persist. We call this mismatch the purpose-to-state semantic gap. The key distinction is that evidence authority is not release authority. We introduce Purpose IR, a bounded typed intermediate representation that compiles natural-language user purpose into an executable semantic boundary for reusable agent state. A Purpose program is an acyclic semantic dataflow graph in which evidence leaves specify task-required semantics, typed dependencies constrain authorized derivations, and declared sinks determine which values or actions may cross the reusable-state boundary. A deterministic compiler constructs and validates the authoritative program, while a typed runtime reconstructs reusable state only from validated sink outputs. Under explicit execution contracts, this design yields release confinement and purpose noninterference, characterizing what factual semantics may be released and which observation differences must become irrelevant to reusable state. Across 1,200 cases spanning LangGraph, CrewAI, and MobileRun, Purpose IR achieves 99.6% Privacy, 83.3% Task, and 83.3% Privacy-Compliant Success (PCS), outperforming the strongest h

6e370d315f72db4a51b3172f.title_original: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
6e370d315f72db4a51b3172f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.

be92ffbc26efff9bc60761f4.title_original: CircuitBreak: Pruning a Sparse Safety Circuit of Neurons
be92ffbc26efff9bc60761f4.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: White-box neuron pruning has shown that refusal in large language models (LLMs) can depend on a small, removable set of feed-forward (FFN) channels. Existing attacks either need carefully paired ``twin'' prompts or score each neuron in isolation. Pruning also has an unavoidable capability cost, so over-removal compounds the loss. TwinBreak removes $1\%$--$5\%$ of parameters and NeuroStrike removes $0.3\%$--$0.7\%$ of neurons in targeted layers. We model safety as a small \emph{circuit} whose neurons contribute jointly rather than independently. We propose \textsc{CircuitBreak}, a neuron-pruning attack that greedily searches for a sparse set of FFN neurons whose joint ablation flips a refusal readout. \textsc{CircuitBreak} re-scores every candidate after the neurons already removed and needs no twin prompts. On ten instruction-tuned models, the greedy search converges after removing $29$--$150$ neurons ($0.0066\%$--$0.0388\%$ of the MLP). The pruned models raise the attack success rate from $2.24\%$/$7.35\%$ to $87.54\%$/$87.54\%$ on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from $8.95\%$/$5.43\%$ to $88.50\%$/$88.18\%$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, as judged by Llama Guard 3 8B on StrongREJECT.

c51ee187f2e62c2a9eb8a055.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose frontier models are large, expensive to run, and increasingly reluctant to engage with authorised defensive- and offensive-security work. We ask the opposite question: how small can a cybersecurity-specialist transformer be while remaining genuinely useful to a security practitioner? We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture, and CT0-Micro, its first incarnation: a compact (~4B-parameter) model built on the open base model, whose backbone is specialised by two-phase on-policy distillation on our Cybersecurity AI (CAI) dataset. CT0 serves two modes from one set of weights: System 1 answers typed security decisions (is this file suspicious, is this request an attack, did the model just refuse) in a single forward pass without generating a token, System 2 is the usual tool-using agent, and a confidence gate spends generation only where the fast path is unsure. Specialisation lifts the agentic path: CT0-Micro solves 21.1% of cybench-subtask against 7.6% for its base, above every open model of comparable footprint and the densest cybersecurity capability per parameter we measured. The fast path is what the architecture buys: CT0-Micro screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise, catches its own refusals at 96.5% accuracy in 47 ms where the model judging itself reaches 76.5% in 254 ms and misses half of them, flags jailbreak requests at AUROC 0.966 in 8 ms, and, generating only for the

45ee06268197d84cc6a768bb.title_original: Beyond User-Side Defenses: Image Protection in Open-Weight Diffusion Models
45ee06268197d84cc6a768bb.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.

53317953c93b1d0990dd8fc3.title_original: Toward Realistic Privacy Risk in FL-Enabled OT Intrusion Detection Systems
53317953c93b1d0990dd8fc3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Operational Technology (OT) environments, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted to train Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) without sharing raw operational data across facilities. However, model updates may still leak sensitive information about industrial processes, creating privacy risks that remain largely invisible within current OT security architectures. Existing reference models, including the Purdue hierarchy, do not explicitly represent the FL learning lifecycle, making privacy leakage difficult to observe and evaluate. To address this gap, we introduce the ML Plane, a novel architectural abstraction that integrates FL workflows within OT systems, enabling visibility of learning-related information flows that are not explicitly represented in traditional OT architectures. Building on the proposed ML Plane, we outline a privacy auditing framework for FL-enabled OT systems. The framework uses Federated Membership Inference Attacks (FedMIA) as an initial assessment mechanism and is being instantiated within a Smart Grid testbed to support the future evaluation of privacy risks under realistic OT deployment constraints.

9ac68cb1c8b5d8f1c7485e17.title_original: Security and robustness analysis of encrypted communications for local home automation: ESPHome Native API and MQTT over TLS 1.3
9ac68cb1c8b5d8f1c7485e17.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) in residential and local automation environments has highlighted the limitations of considering the internal network as an inherently trusted domain. Man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks, such as ARP spoofing, can allow traffic interception or manipulation when communications lack appropriate confidentiality, integrity, and authentication mechanisms. This paper presents a systematized review of the security mechanisms used by two communication alternatives between ESP-family microcontrollers and the Home Assistant platform: MQTT protected through TLS 1.3 and the ESPHome Native API, whose encryption is based on the Noise Protocol Framework using the Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 pattern. The analysis considers four dimensions: cryptographic robustness, attack surface, implementation complexity, and resource consumption. The review identifies significant differences resulting from the architecture and cryptographic model of each alternative. TLS 1.3 provides a standardized framework compatible with public-key infrastructure and formal identity management, though it introduces greater configuration complexity and computational overhead during session establishment. The ESPHome Native API employs a more specialized scheme with lower operational complexity, eliminates dynamic algorithm negotiation, and uses ChaCha20-Poly1305. The resource-consumption analysis relies on measurements pub

331db9fb163f3ee2d54bb2e2.title_original: Think Locally Before Computing Jointly: Efficient Secure Multi-Party Computation via Maximizing Local Processing
331db9fb163f3ee2d54bb2e2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties evaluate a function over private inputs without revealing them. In garbled-circuit (GC) protocols, prior optimization has largely treated the number of non-linear gates, especially AND gates, as a proxy for cryptographic cost, and has focused on minimizing multiplicative complexity. We identify an orthogonal source of savings: a gate need not be garbled when one party knows or can locally compute its inputs; that party can evaluate it outside the secure protocol, even when the gate is non-linear. We introduce ownership-aware optimization for GC-based MPC, which minimizes non-linear gates requiring joint evaluation rather than total non-linear gates. We formalize this objective in a cost model and implement a compiler-integrated, gate-level framework that restructures Boolean circuits to increase party-local computation while preserving secure-computation semantics. The method is automated and general-purpose, and composes with existing multiplicative-complexity optimization. Experiments show that it reduces jointly evaluated computation and improves end-to-end GC performance on circuits with party-local structure, revealing protocol-cost savings missed by conventional GC cost models.

4c083bbd5e9e6f1b63a8bb13.title_original: SEAL-DT: An End-to-End Security Engineering and Assurance Framework for Cross-Domain Digital Twins
4c083bbd5e9e6f1b63a8bb13.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber-physical systems connect physical processes, software, networks and organizations. Securing them requires a clear account of what happened, what was observed, which actions were authorized and what evidence supports each decision. Digital Twin (DT) descriptions often fail to explain how these elements stay consistent, blur the distinction between physical events and uncertain observations, or detach simulation results from their requirements and assumptions. This paper presents SEAL-DT (Security Engineering and Assurance Lifecycle for Digital Twins), a structured approach to building and evaluating secure DTs. It brings entity definitions, process models, deterministic simulations, data contracts, evidence records, automated tests and reproducible results into one connected model. The main contribution is an end-to-end DT security framework, spanning scenario definition, entity/process modelling, simulation, security decision logic, evidence handling, validation and reproducible reporting. Security decisions and simulation results thus trace back to their data, assumptions and requirements. A DT is more than a copy of system state: it states what it can observe, how accurate and current its information is, where it came from and which decisions it may support. We demonstrate SEAL-DT in five scenarios: Car2X protection, passive IoT-device detection, an industrial control surrogate, lawful acquisition in a smart home, and me

f27ad373f855645f21b6cd69.title_original: Tight End-to-End Accounting for Differentially Private Synthetic Data
f27ad373f855645f21b6cd69.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differentially private (DP) pipelines often combine heterogeneous mechanisms, yet their guarantees are best analyzed using different notions of privacy (e.g., bounded range, zCDP, ADP). When composing them, we have to analyze the guarantees through a reduced common representation that loses accounting precision. This issue is particularly relevant in DP synthetic data generation, where data preprocessing, generation algorithms, and DP-SGD could appear within the same pipeline. We develop novel tools for tight end-to-end accounting of such compositions using privacy loss distributions (PLD), $f$-DP, and Gaussian DP (GDP). In particular, we derive PLD and GDP analyses of bounded-range mechanisms such as the Exponential mechanism. Building on these theoretical results, we introduce AIM-GDP, a GDP-native variant of AIM (a state-of-the-art DP synthetic data mechanism) that enables easy composability with complex pipelines via PLD, attack-aware risk calibration, and tight end-to-end auditing while consistently achieving better utility; and MixCal, an algorithm for calibrating adaptive mixed compositions using PLD accounting. Overall, our tools enable tighter end-to-end accounting and thus less noise at the same privacy level in DP synthetic data pipelines.

3a70d662ecc8288b2ef4daba.title_original: TRAP: Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing for Automated LLM Jailbreaking
3a70d662ecc8288b2ef4daba.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that circumvent their safety guardrails, making the identification of these vulnerabilities important for understanding and mitigating model weaknesses. Existing automated jailbreak methods explore prompt candidates or reuse attack experience, but generally do not learn over a persistent hierarchy that connects related jailbreak strategies, such as role-play, encoding, and obfuscation. This leaves the relationships among reusable strategies underused in guiding adaptive attack selection. We present Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing (TRAP), a hierarchical framework for automated jailbreak strategy discovery that requires only black-box access to the target LLM. TRAP organizes established jailbreak methods and successful attack templates into a semantic strategy tree, connecting broad attack approaches to concrete, reusable strategies. A reinforcement-learning policy based on a tree-structured gradient bandit explores this tree and uses evaluator feedback to update strategy preferences along each selected path. The policy retains these preferences across attack objectives, allowing experience from earlier attempts to guide subsequent strategy selection. Retrieval-augmented prompt construction translates the selected strategy into an attack for the current objective using relevant successful examples. Experiments on AdvBench across seven aligned L

6b629835b034883575aeeddf.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers are increasingly deployed to optimize quality, latency, and cost through dynamic model selection and request rewriting. However, a compromised router can cause ineligible selection on the control plane, unendorsed rewriting or unfaithful relay on the data plane, undermining LLM routing integrity. We present VeriRouter, a verifiable LLM routing framework. Under an endorsed public context binding a private semantic index and rewrite banks, VeriRouter combines ZK proofs with a provider-issued serving certificate to establish integrity across both planes while keeping the router's private routing assets hidden from clients. For model selection, we design an efficient ZK proof for semantic search. For rewriting, local checks enforce message preservation and additions from committed banks. On real-world workloads, VeriRouter's model-selection and rewrite proofs average 21.92~s and 4.24~s, yielding 1,307$\times$ and 101$\times$ speedups over the fastest completing baselines. Relative to serving without verification, VeriRouter adds only 4.08 s under per-turn selection and 0.11 s under session-pinned selection.

886b53daf4eaba3bdcd9f94e.title_original: BrowseSafe++: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts, Languages, and Browser Views
886b53daf4eaba3bdcd9f94e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Browser agents need to make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users while consuming untrusted webpages, creating opportunities for malicious instructions embedded in webpages to redirect legitimate tasks. We introduce BrowseSafe++, which extends BrowseSafe from 14,719 pages to 38,675 pairs of pages. Most of its prompt injections were observed in the wild on production websites. We keep each injection unchanged and rewrite the sensitive parts of the page around it to protect privacy. Each attacked page has a clean copy of the same page as its control. Both are provided as HTML, Markdown, an accessibility tree, and a screenshot. Every pair includes a user task and its expected answer. The benchmark includes twelve types of websites, from news articles to shared documents and forums, with 24 attack types appearing in 18 different locations on a page. We use these paired pages to train BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots. Both achieve higher F1 scores than the detector based on frontier models, while keeping false-positive rates on benign pages and inference cost low. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises benchmark injections from browser-agent feedback, and attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly reach up to 95.41% success once adapted.

0715550d08a3d9b4afdf0bb6.title_original: Discovery or Memorization? A Faithful Benchmark for Real-World Business-Logic Vulnerability Discovery
0715550d08a3d9b4afdf0bb6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advancement of cybersecurity agents in vulnerability discovery has increased the need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities accurately. However, synthetic benchmarks lack realism, real-life benchmarks are prone to contamination, and many existing benchmarks have already been saturated by current models. We therefore set out to develop a benchmark that is realistic, reproducible, resistant to contamination, and challenging. Our key insight is that real-life business-logic vulnerabilities are subtle and exercise complex application interactions, making them naturally demanding. The difficulty lies in specifying evaluation criteria precise enough to faithfully measure model capabilities while keeping the tasks free of data-leakage. We introduce AnonVul, a cross-language benchmark of 132 application-level business-logic vulnerabilities, built by a semi-automated pipeline that anonymizes each task, injects oracles from expert-written specifications, and differentially verifies proof-of-concept exploits. The benchmark spans nine languages, with two evaluation tracks on black-box and grey-box settings, where each task runs in a sandbox with specialized oracles embedded in key exploitation steps. We evaluate six state-of-the-art vulnerability-discovery agents on the AnonVul benchmark, measuring discovery success, cost-effectiveness, anonymization sensitivity, oracle validity, and failure modes. Our results show that

6587e315dd6f0b4fac1b28f5.title_original: Extending Layered Attestation into ARM Application Run-Times
6587e315dd6f0b4fac1b28f5.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern mobile and edge platforms provide hardware-backed attestation of application and platform integrity at load-time. However, they offer little support once application execution begins. We present ARA, an Application-Runtime Anchor for ARM that extends this load-time chain of trust into execution. ARA bootstraps from the underlying ARM platform Root of Trust (RoT) through a measured loading chain and establishes an attested protected run-time within the application address space using recently introduced ARM Permission Overlay Extensions (POE). The resulting run-time domain can host programmable RoTs for Measurement and Storage (RTM/RTS), enabling application run-time integrity verification, attestation evidence generation, and protected use of secrets while retaining efficient access to application run-time state. As exemplary uses, we instantiate ARA for protected media decryption and application control flow measurement. Our prototype and evaluation show that ARA supports frequent run-time RoT-backed operations at near in-process cost, with roughly 10x and 50x lower overhead than out-of-process equivalents. This offers a practical bridge from layered attestation to application run-time trusted computing on ARM.

5e1380e515283bd2bbaf739b.title_original: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
5e1380e515283bd2bbaf739b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following. (1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}}<1/2$ such that, for $k\ge c_{\mathrm{bh}}n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to arbitrary one-bit leakage from every share. The best previous threshold was $0.668n$. (2) For every fixed $0<\delta<1/2$ and $k\ge(1/2+\delta)n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to $\left\lfloor\frac{\delta}{24}\log_2 n\right\rfloor$ bits of arbitrary local leakage per share. By a recent attack, this number of bits is optimal up to a constant factor depending on $\delta$. (3) For every fixed threshold rate $c>0$ and $k\ge cn$, Shamir sharing is resilient to quadratic-residue leakage and to almost all local leakage functions of up to $\eta_c\log_2 p$ bits, for a constant $\eta_c>0$. All three results follow from one analytic framework, which we develop for generalized Reed--Solomon codes: local leakage from a uniform codeword is statistically close to the same leakage from independent uniform field elements. The framework expresses the leakage distance as the norm of a function on the leakage outputs. The Efron--Stein decomposition splits this function into orthogonal components indexed by supports of dual codewords. Two tools bound the components: list recovery

36d887a79b5d1d5cd8a3e743.title_original: Beyond Model Scaling: Rethinking Sequence Construction for Transformer-based Network Intrusion Detection
36d887a79b5d1d5cd8a3e743.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformer-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) have shown strong potential for detecting multi-stage cyberattacks, yet most methods construct input sequences using fixed temporalization schemes rather than treating sequence construction as a systems design decision. In flow-based intrusion detection, timestamp-based windowing often fragments related attack activities while merging unrelated communications, reducing the behavioral context available to transformers. We present a unified pipeline abstraction that decomposes transformer-based NIDS into four design dimensions (traffic representation, temporalization, transformer backbone, and prediction aggregation) and propose session-coherent temporalization, which constructs sequences from communication sessions instead of fixed time windows. Experiments on three complementary intrusion detection datasets show that temporalization is the dominant factor governing transformer performance: session-coherent temporalization more than doubles Macro-F1 over timestamp-based windowing, enabling lightweight transformers to achieve up to 0.95 Macro-F1 at substantially higher inference throughput than pretrained models. We further vary the transformer size from 0.65M to 3.38M parameters and find that larger transformer models provide no measurable accuracy improvement despite substantially higher computational cost, while zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation shows only modest gai

2e15d5f932a4ba282eabeff1.title_original: Provenance and Authorization in Autobiographical Language Models
2e15d5f932a4ba282eabeff1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autobiographical language models may draw on archives containing observations, quotations, emotional reports, and earlier model outputs. Cryptographic authentication can preserve an archive while leaving these sources semantically conflated. We formulate this gap as a computer-security problem: narrative content must not silently become consent or alter an authorized decision rule. We define typed records, authenticated attestations, a separate policy channel, and admissible views. Under explicit assumptions, we give a standard integrity reduction and a noninterference argument, characterize the information required by exact decision-preserving summaries, and show why passive history and fixed-point convergence need not identify a preferred action. Alpay Algebra supplies a comparative language for iterative memory without being a premise of the proofs. Sociology of religious affiliation, source-monitoring psychology, and self-determination theory motivate distinctions in a bounded Latter-day Saint vignette. A separate, reproducible pilot uses a frozen public language model on 32 wholly synthetic cases across 576 paired conditions. It compares flattened records, source labels, and an explicit admission gate under contradictory summary repetition. The study concerns computational attribution and authorization, not the motives or psychology of the people in the vignette.

9350e18dafb9d137d720d2c9.title_original: Standing, Not Truth: Who May Say What About Whom in Agentic Selection
9350e18dafb9d137d720d2c9.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software agents increasingly choose on a user's behalf among competing offerings described by the parties who benefit. A lawful participant, publishing under its own identity, compromising no channel and issuing no instruction, can move that choice with a single false factual claim about a competing offering. Across twelve published defenses spanning the three placements a check can occupy, none separates it from marketing. Each accepts it for a reason correct on its own: its origin is a lawful channel, its influence is evidence meant to decide, its action serves the user's goal. None establishes that the publisher was entitled to speak about a competitor, each exclusion stated by the defenses' own authors. Disclosure does not replace enforcement: re-rendering every description as attributed speech leaves the attack at 72/72, the agent repeating the attribution and reasoning from it. The missing relation is standing: whether a claimant's bound identity entitles it to assert about a claim's subject. A publisher may say what its own package does. It has no standing to say a competitor's package is frozen, and the difference is decidable without settling whether either is true. Deciding it needs the one fact prose extraction does not recover, who spoke, which a catalogue binds to every entry and then drops. The check is quiet on honest traffic, flagging 0.9% of natural pairs in two corpora. Used as a gate it stops 130 of 131 landed

bc6325e9e8d16a72c9b99d3a.title_original: Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference on Financial Transaction Graphs via Homomorphic Encryption
bc6325e9e8d16a72c9b99d3a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) in financial networks requires modeling transaction patterns that span multiple institutions. In practice, however, banks cannot share account and transaction features due to strict privacy regulations. We propose a privacy-preserving graph neural network (GNN) inference framework tailored to this multi-bank setting. A central server holds the graph connectivity and pretrained model weights in plaintext, while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted. Inference is then carried out entirely on encrypted features under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, so that no plaintext transaction features or predictions are exposed to the server. The key to making this practical is an edge-centric GNN architecture, wherein message passing is expressed through operations on node--edge incidence matrices. This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as \textbf{5.31} seconds, while per-transaction latency can

eac5517991cf5de232c7c4d0.title_original: BALLAST: Physics-Aware Moving Target Defense for Industrial Control Systems Using a Digital Twin Safety Oracle
eac5517991cf5de232c7c4d0.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial Control Systems run on static network configurations, which leaves an attacker unlimited time to map the plant. Moving Target Defense answers this by shuffling addresses, but almost every published scheme never checks whether the reconfiguration will itself disturb the physical process it protects, so the defense can destabilise a control loop or trip an actuator. We present BALLAST, which places a learned Digital Twin between the security policy and the plant as a safety oracle. A physics-informed LSTM surrogate forecasts the physical effect of a candidate network change, a reinforcement learning agent trades security entropy against process stability, and a connection-draining handover lets in-flight Modbus transactions complete before the old mapping is withdrawn. An explicit shield rejects any action whose predicted trajectory would leave the safe operating envelope. On the SWaT water treatment testbed, Ballast cut the success rate of an adversary's reconnaissance sweep by 85 percent and recorded no safety violation across 50 runs, a 95 percent upper bound of 5.8 percent on the violation rate, against five violations and a tracking error 19 times larger for RL-MTD, the closest published analogue to our design. Measured against the strongest baseline on the physical metrics, a threshold-triggered scheme that itself records one violation rather than RL-MTD's five, Ballast still improves the tracking error by a facto

10d51cb696d0753763039a7f.title_original: Jev-Guard: Fast Routing and Auditing Agent Actions over Editable Policy Trees
10d51cb696d0753763039a7f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent harnesses require a low-latency guardrail model together with customizable audit policies. However, deploying an auto-regressive guardrail model remains challenging: such models incur high inference latency and are often poorly aligned with customized policies. To address these problems, we present Jev-Guard, a unified model for safety classification and policy routing. We further construct a policy tree over which Jev-Guard performs routing, spanning diverse domains including content moderation, cybersecurity, privacy, and legal compliance. Specifically, Jev-Guard first navigates the policy tree to select the applicable audit policy given the caller's audit context, and then performs safety classification conditioned on the retrieved policies. On 7,033 evaluation cases, Jev-Guard achieves 93.72\% safety accuracy, a mean latency of 58ms, and 93.10\% hierarchical routing accuracy. The full routing-and-classification pipeline averages 240ms. Furthermore, we integrate Jev-Guard into the Hermes harness framework. Across agent trajectories, its separate permission gate cuts mean review time per task from 4.80s for an SFT-LLM judge to 1.33s, with no policy violations are observed for either guard.

2a88593372f6df69c35f2016.title_original: Pin It on Anyone: Certified Targeted Displacement of Multi-Bit LLM Watermarks Without the Key
2a88593372f6df69c35f2016.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-bit watermarking embeds a message, typically an account identifier, into LLM output so that harmful text can be traced to its origin. We show an attack technique that allows to alter the watermarking message. This allows to, for example, exchange the embedded account ID to an arbitrary different one. The attacker mainly needs access to a few accounts for generating LLM output and model logits, but crucially not the secret key used to watermark. The attacker then rewrites the text, keeping its meaning, so that the watermarking message decoder recovers the watermarking message embedded by the attacker. We are, to our knowledge, the first to propose such an attack, which we call a targeted displacement. Theoretically, we present upper and lower bounds on the probability of our attack succeeding. This bound depends on the number of accounts the attacker has access to, the length of the message and some characteristics of the given text. Our attack can succeed whenever we can bound the ambiguity of the generated text well enough. Empirically, we test our attack technique against five watermarking methods and four LLMs. Attack success tracks our predicted bounds, allowing us to alter watermarking messages in almost all cases with high accuracy, given enough accounts. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Batorskq/PinIt.

fa22fb3df676b8c26954a32f.title_original: HULK: An Efficient Algorithm for Enabling Fast Bulk Bitwise Operations on Homomorphically Encrypted Data
fa22fb3df676b8c26954a32f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A wide range of important cloud applications, e.g., database analytics, graph analytics, and genome analysis, spend a considerable amount of time performing bulk bitwise operations (e.g., AND, OR, XOR). These applications often operate on highly sensitive data, making data privacy a critical concern. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without requiring decryption, ensuring privacy in untrusted and shared environments. We analyze 13 end-to-end applications across three domains (healthcare, graph, and database analytics) and observe that bulk bitwise operations take 62-100% of the execution time of the healthcare and graph workloads. The key problem is that existing HE approaches perform them with high-latency homomorphic operations (e.g., multiplication or lookup tables) and significantly increase the data size. Our goal is to enable fast bulk bitwise operations on homomorphically encrypted data by designing an efficient HE algorithm that reduces the use of these costly operations. To this end, we propose HULK, which performs two key steps: (1) it constructs bulk bitwise operations using low-cost homomorphic additions, which compute the Hamming weight of the encrypted operand bits in every slot of a packed ciphertext without any homomorphic multiplication, and (2) it decodes the result of an AND, OR, or XOR from the Hamming weight with a single indicator polynomial, keeping the result in the

ad5be382c883de57b86e0f4d.title_original: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
ad5be382c883de57b86e0f4d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmark

9b331acf3029b8a67b5d3f28.title_original: Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
9b331acf3029b8a67b5d3f28.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher u

3aa7eb026dd2cd0cc1e52f37.title_original: Prompt-Segmentation Meets ROI Encryption: Fine-Grained Video Protection Based on Diffusion Isolation
3aa7eb026dd2cd0cc1e52f37.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Region-of-interest (ROI) selective encryption in H.265/HEVC aims to protect sensitive content while preserving the utility of non-ROI regions. Existing coding-unit (CU)-level approaches still suffer from substantial encryption redundancy for two reasons. First, existing approaches map object-detection bounding boxes to CUs, producing regular rectangular regions, which poorly match the shape of irregular ROI boundaries, such as facial contours. Second, their coding-tree-unit (CTU)-based diffusion isolation expands the protected footprint in fixed $64\times64$ blocks, causing encryption-induced distortion to spread over a large number of non-ROI pixels. To address the aforementioned shortcomings, we propose a prompt segmentation-guided CU-level ROI encryption algorithm, which mainly consists of two core components. The first component is a prompt segmentation-guided fine-grained ROI encryption pipeline. It maps pixel-level ROI masks to CUs according to an ROI-overlap threshold, refines boundary CUs to $8\times8$ granularity, and applies format-compliant encryption to multiple syntax elements in the mapped ROI CUs. The second is a dual diffusion isolation strategy to address the encryption diffusion problem. For spatial isolation, the encoder refines non-ROI boundary regions into $8\times8$ CUs and uses PCM mode to bypass intra-frame prediction. For temporal isolation, it removes motion-vector candidates whose reference blocks over

7663d0eb067df1dce3834b8c.title_original: X.js: A Live Benchmark for Node.js Taint-Style Vulnerabilities
7663d0eb067df1dce3834b8c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: JavaScript vulnerabilities in npm packages pose a significant risk to the Node.js ecosystem, and a growing body of work aims to detect, exploit, and mitigate them. Studying and evaluating this work requires up-to-date collections of real vulnerabilities, yet the most commonly used datasets stop recording vulnerabilities in 2022. We present X.js, a live benchmark of real-world Node.js taint-style vulnerabilities covering code and command injection, prototype pollution, and path traversal. Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X.js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X.js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X.js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node.js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.

b1b44d2bce1af455d6b0ef57.title_original: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
b1b44d2bce1af455d6b0ef57.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.

c32021bf6276800fcc5af1e3.title_original: ARACDE: Retrofitting Databases with ABAC using External Authorization Engines
c32021bf6276800fcc5af1e3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a methodology for decoupling the authorization logic of a relational database from its core data management engine, enabling specification of advanced access control policies with minimal changes to the code base. Our decoupled authorization architecture, which we call ARCADE, externalizes access request resolution to a formally verifiable policy engine (e.g., Cedar), while the database itself enforces those decisions. We showcase the capabilities of ARCADE on two widely popular open-source databases, namely MySQL and PostgreSQL. Purpose built lightweight plugins add an Attribute-based Access Control (ABAC) layer that augments the native discretionary and role-based access control capabilities of these databases. ARCADE supports highly expressive policies using attributes of subjects, objects, and the environment, and the use of Cedar enables easy auditing and verification of the specified policies. It follows a design principle that mitigates potential risks in segregating authorization from the database core through low footprint, network isolation, and a policy composition methodology that does not negate any native authorization. Experiments on TPC-C, TPC-B, and a custom workload show that ARCADE incurs negligible performance overhead, for instance, less than 3.9% throughput penalty for MySQL (1.3% for PostgreSQL) on industry standard TPC-C benchmark.

f0d7499af79525a29a04a2d7.title_original: AegisAsync: Symbolic Async-Event Simulation for Risks in Python Asynchronous Programs
f0d7499af79525a29a04a2d7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security and robustness risks in Python async programs depend on event order, object identity, and execution after exceptions or cancellation. Detecting these risks requires connecting related operations across function calls and tracking their effects along execution paths. We present AegisAsync, a bytecode-based analysis of Python async risks for CPython 3.10-3.14. Its Async Event Transition Graph combines bytecode control flow, resolved calls, async events, and symbolic object relations. Bounded path-local simulation tracks event order and object states and explores cancellation at await suspensions. Six detector plugins evaluate the resulting traces and states to produce candidates with supporting witnesses. On AsyncBench, our benchmark of 180 labeled risks, AegisAsync detects all labeled risks with zero false positives on each of the five versions. Across five path budgets on 2,500 PyPI package versions, source review confirms 457 of 910 AegisAsync candidate records (50.2%), representing 457 unique bugs; across three flake8-async samples, 70 of 2,187 review judgments are confirmed (3.2%). By submission, 166 PoCs reproduce AegisAsync findings, and we have reported 157 bugs to developers, of which 16 have been confirmed and fixed.

5d171432561d934e91800f77.title_original: Proof-Gated Publication: Verify-Before-Commit Content Integrity for Serverless Data-Mesh Lakehouses
5d171432561d934e91800f77.excerpt: arXiv:2608.14643v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated data meshes give domain teams ownership of their data products, and serverless compute is an attractive substrate for domain-owned writes. Both trends weaken correctness at publication. Open table formats such as Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake guarantee that a commit is atomic and that readers see an isolated snapshot, but not that the rows persisted equal the rows the job intended to write; publication is decided from the writer's exit status. A serverless job that silently drops a partition, truncates a file on retry, or duplicates a chunk still produces a valid, atomic, isolated, and wrong snapshot. This paper presents PVDM, a proof-gated publication protocol with four phases: Physical (write to rollbackable staging), Verify (a keyed multiset proof that written content equals declared intent, stored by an independent notary), Durable (replay completed chunks across serverless retries), and Metadata (commit the catalog last, only if the proof passed). Metadata commits only if the proof passes, so a failing proof yields no consumer-visible snapshot. The verification primitive is a keyed, incremental multiset hash over identity and content projections, telling missing or duplicated rows apart from corrupted values. A dependency-free reference gate, a thirty-case adversarial suite, and a reproducible benchmark catch eight thousand of eight thousand injected faults up to one million rows with no false blocks. We also ru

3fee38b31c376f2fafcf74dc.title_original: Building Trustworthy Household Robots through Open-World Safety
3fee38b31c376f2fafcf74dc.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14034v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation models are expanding robot capabilities, enabling robots to handle more diverse objects, follow sophisticated instructions, and operate in complex environments. These advances bring us to a future in which robots become part of everyday household life. However, cluttered, dynamic household environments also expose robots to unfamiliar objects, tasks, and interactions, making reliable zero-shot task completion an ongoing challenge for robotics research. From a security perspective, we argue for open-world safety: household robots should preserve specified safety requirements in unseen situations, including when they cannot complete the requested task. Safety protections must account for context and interactions that persist across actions and tasks. In this position paper, we examine why existing safety methods can fail to provide this protection. Protection can fail through misinterpreted context, overlooked past interactions, or stopping and recovery strategies that become unsafe under unfamiliar conditions. We therefore propose a research agenda to specify, learn, and ground safety requirements, enforce them with reliable recovery, and evaluate the generalization of such protections. We call for household robots whose safety protections remain reliable beyond the situations, context, and history used to train and develop them, to achieve open-world safety.

74e2e6501e4f9af9469e7c3c.title_original: RoboFake: Are Deepfake Detectors Ready for Humanoid Face Robots?
74e2e6501e4f9af9469e7c3c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14269v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humanoid face robots can now move their lips in sync with speech and show detailed facial expressions. Give such a robot the face of a real person and drive it with generated speech, and you get a face forgery that happens in front of the camera: the camera records a real object, and no pixel is edited. We call this a RoboFake. In this paper we ask what current deepfake detectors do when they see a robot face. We test six public detectors trained on FaceForensics++ on video of a physical lip-syncing face robot, on a synthesized video of the same robot, and on rendered robot faces. All thresholds are fixed on FaceForensics++, and every result is compared with real human faces that went through the same processing as the robot videos. At a threshold that flags 5% of real faces, three detectors flag almost every physical robot frame, while two flag fewer than 7%. A matched human control and masking show that the response comes from the face, not from the processing or the background. However, it does not track synthesis: with only the face visible, three of the six detectors give the physical robot a higher fake score than its synthesized video. The response is also fragile, and light JPEG compression is enough to push most robot frames below the threshold for some detectors. Our results suggest that current detectors flag today's robots because their faces do not look human, not because they recognize a forgery. We release our e

51a8cb37fda7f9c6bbf96f58.title_original: DS and AMDS Symbol-Pair Codes from Three Families of Simple Root Cyclic Codes
51a8cb37fda7f9c6bbf96f58.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14435v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symbol-pair distances of simple-root cyclic codes are important for evaluating error correction performance under overlapping pair read channels. In this paper, we construct three families of simple-root cyclic codes over finite fields of odd characteristic via generator polynomials. For length \(2q+2\), the minimum symbol-pair distance is \(10\) for every odd prime power \(q\ge 7\), established by excluding invalid support configurations. For length \(4q-4\), when \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) and finite field constraints hold, it is \(9\) or \(10\). For length \(2(q-1)\), reciprocal-polynomial analysis shows it is \(11\) or \(12\). All obtained codes are MDS or AMDS symbol-pair codes.

c5ea861988a5d17d5b7a7b98.title_original: Declared but Unaccountable: Measuring the Seller-Identity Gap in Advertising Supply-Chain Transparency
c5ea861988a5d17d5b7a7b98.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14661v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public advertising transparency relies on a minimum accountability condition: an account authorized by a publisher in ads.txt or app-ads.txt should appear in the applicable sellers.json registry. When an available registry omits the declared seller ID, the authorization remains visible and machine-readable, but its public verification path breaks. We call this failure the seller-identity gap. We measure the gap using 233.4 million normalized advertising-transparency records and an absent-only, coverage-aware evidence rule. A declaration enters the numerator only when the applicable registry is available and omits its seller ID; unavailable, malformed, confidential, and other non-evaluable states remain separate. The resulting row-level floor is 24.25% in a high-popularity, low-removal reference population and 30.71% among publishers associated with at least 100 copyright-removal requests, a 6.45 percentage-point increase. The gap then remains near one third at stricter cumulative thresholds. Standardizing the populations to common weights over 1,469 shared ad systems reduces the primary contrast to 4.65 points: about 72% remains within systems, while 28% forms a composition-associated residual. We connect these population estimates to recurring seller-account coordinates, byte-identical declaration configurations, and provenance-bearing case packets. We frame this declaration-centered investigative use of public advertising re

29db3d127f3d7359747defbe.title_original: (Implicitly) Characterizing Probabilistic Polynomial Time as Used in Cryptography
29db3d127f3d7359747defbe.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we show how a recently introduced $\lambda$-calculus for randomized computation, called $\lambda\mathbf{BLL}$, can accurately capture the notions of first- and second-order polytime computations used in cryptographic definitions and proofs.
