These results, spelled out in the style of so-called \emph{implicit computational complexity}, imply that $\lambda\mathbf{BLL}$ is sufficiently powerful to express experiments and adversaries as used in cryptography, and that reductions, when formulated within the calculus, are guaranteed to be complexity-preserving. Remarkably, while polynomial-time soundness holds for the full calculus, polynomial-time completeness already follows in presence of a minimal finite set of basic functions.

9e3e46398985c90139d7e2a8.title_original: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
9e3e46398985c90139d7e2a8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authori

a11650f376bc78e9578345bb.title_original: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
a11650f376bc78e9578345bb.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15177v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.

bfedba7fac1e3f939d86c10c.title_original: Robust Detection of Directional Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks for Radiological Imaging
bfedba7fac1e3f939d86c10c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15628v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning is now central to radiology, helping detect changes on X-rays, CTs, and MRIs. However, these systems are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks - small, crafted perturbations that mislead models while appearing unchanged to humans. Such errors risk missed cancers or false positives. Studies show over 90% attack success on medical scans. Almost 30% of US hospitals use AI in imaging in 2023. Thus, an effective method of detecting such attacks and their directionality is crucial to ensure the credibility and reliability of medical systems based on DNNs. We propose a novel detection framework that leverages subsequent attacks using random noise to identify adversarial perturbations. Our approach uses the analysis of variations in the Sigmoid function to distinguish genuine medical images from adversarially manipulated ones. Specifically, we compare prediction differences between clean and attacked images, as well as between different adversarially altered versions, to improve detection accuracy. We evaluated our method on three popular medical datasets including 'Chest X-Ray Images for Classification', 'Retinal Fundus Multi-disease Image Dataset' and 'Brain Tumor Dataset' under various attack scenarios, including random noise. Our framework achieved up to 99.8% ACC in identifying adversarial directional attacks, significantly outperforming existing defense mechanisms. It consistently identified adversarial samples

d23915120523519821199388.title_original: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
d23915120523519821199388.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15721v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver's native safety behavior as safety incompatibility. Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo, a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.

2963d5ca7efc3cf86426bb54.title_original: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Testing and Automation of Open RAN Systems: GNG-OTA Framework
2963d5ca7efc3cf86426bb54.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15872v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open Radio Access Networks (O-RAN) empower operators with choice and customization through their disaggregated and interoperable architecture. However, ensuring interoperability in O-RAN presents challenges due to complex testing environments and evolving specifications. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing the Generative AI and Graph Neural Network-based Open RAN Testing and Automation (GNG-OTA) framework. GNG-OTA utilizes state-of-the-art AI techniques including generative AI, natural language processing, and graph neural networks to enable accurate, reliable, efficient, and automatic O-RAN interoperability and performance testing.

dda7d11f52b299161de487b5.title_original: Not All Challenges Are Equal: Evaluating Interactive Liveness Detection Against Real-Time Face Swaps
dda7d11f52b299161de487b5.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16417v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Remote identity verification assumes that a camera stream shows a live person, yet public real-time face-swap tools can replace that person before the stream reaches the verifier. Passive deepfake detectors generalize poorly to new generators, while interactive challenges are often selected without evidence of which gestures expose current attacks. We evaluate randomized gesture challenges in 108 live sessions with six subjects, 24 impersonated identities, and two face-swap tools, DeepFaceLive and FaceFusion, injected through a virtual camera. The static calibration segment reaches a session-level AUC of 0.878 with a frozen UCF spatial detector, while the mean across the active-gesture windows reaches 0.988. Pose and combined gestures have the highest point estimates, whereas expressions show no clear improvement. Hand occlusion against FaceFusion, configured with an occlusion mask, scores below the static baseline. The end-to-end time required to satisfy the validator also distinguishes attacks from genuine sessions, achieving a session-level AUC of 0.732, although this signal includes synthesis and transport delays. These results show that challenge sets should be tested against current attack configurations and that response time can provide an additional, deployment-specific signal.

b78908bd3ed91b488ebb68d3.title_original: Revisiting Fast Tendermint: An Agreement Violation and Two Repairs
b78908bd3ed91b488ebb68d3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16442v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fast Tendermint reduces Tendermint's good-case latency to two communication steps for n>=5f+1. We show that its published round-change rule violates Agreement: one Byzantine process suffices for every f>=1, and for f>=2 two Byzantine processes suffice without double signing. The failure occurs when a process advances past a round without recording the value that may have been decided there. The Quint specification that accompanies the protocol does not allow this kind of round skipping and is not affected; the violation lies in the published pseudocode. We present two repairs. Walk requires a process to leave each round on a quorum of that round's precommits and to precommit before leaving. It keeps the recorded valid state and removes the wait after a precommit quorum. Justify carries the evidence needed to accept a proposal in the proposal itself, removing both the recorded valid state and the proposer's synchronization wait. Both satisfy Agreement and Validity under asynchrony and Termination under the partially synchronous gossip model of Tendermint and Fast Tendermint. Both retain proposal timeouts. The main text presents the executions that violate Agreement and explains the two repairs. The appendices provide proofs, a brief comparison with other round-change designs, and an extension to chains.

5e4e210c858b554c6304f79d.title_original: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
5e4e210c858b554c6304f79d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16770v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Digital Twin (DT) combined with reinforcement learning (RL) can support adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making by comparing expected and observed network behavior. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network. For each action, the same channel simulator is evaluated under an attack-free and an attacked configuration. Receiver-level residuals are combined with spatial jamming footprints and accumulated to form a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into an aggregated state, a belief-concentration reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. The BGQL scheme is compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random under matched attacker sets. Across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs in four configurations, with the number of active jammers supplied to every method, BGQL achieves mean aggregate full-band link-rate scores of approximately 437.4--564.2~Mbit/s and rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37--76.79~Mbit/J. Its detection accuracy is 100\% in one-jammer configurations and approximately 78\%--81\% in two-jammer configurations. BGQL requires approximately 80--130~s per run, compared with 5--14~s for SARSA, reflecting evaluation of 625 beam pairs during exploratory steps. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided lea

ae94a7d57ab8b3edde8f237c.title_original: The Right to Be Forgotten under Correlation: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs
ae94a7d57ab8b3edde8f237c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17088v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study privacy-preserving algorithms that redact information from a correlated dataset. The goal is to reduce the information leakage about sensitive parts. We analytically characterize the optimal tradeoff between privacy (leakage through correlation) and utility (number of redactions) for local mechanisms and binary Markovian correlations. Our result shows how to decompose the mechanism design problem into a sequence of local mechanism design problems and reveals their sequential relation. The optimal mechanism is the solution to a Finite-Horizon Deterministic Markov Decision Process.

c1913bf5e1bde8a2e659d1f4.title_original: Can R\'enyi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
c1913bf5e1bde8a2e659d1f4.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17120v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as R\'enyi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on R\'enyi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved R\'enyi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a R\'enyi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.

396a3c99327acefe76cf9a1c.title_original: SSM-Attack: Learning Where to Perturb for Black-Box Face Privacy
396a3c99327acefe76cf9a1c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17323v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Face recognition systems are deployed widely enough that a photograph shared online can be matched without its subject's consent. Generator-based protection methods rely on heavy pretrained backbones, multi-stage inference or visible semantic edits. We introduce SSM-Attack, a black-box face privacy framework built on Selective State Space Models. Rather than synthesizing the perturbation, the state-space model predicts in one linear-time pass a spatial allocation of the perturbation budget, marking which facial locations carry identity evidence; a short projected refinement then sets the values within this per-pixel budget. Against published benchmark results, SSM-Attack attains the highest average black-box attack success rate on all three evaluation sets: 87.10 percent on CelebA-HQ, 86.90 on LADN and 81.15 on FFHQ, the last from a network that never saw that dataset. The allocation network holds 5.73 million parameters, or 16.13 million with the frozen networks used by its quality terms. Under the same cap of 0.10 on the maximum per-pixel change, allocation improves structural similarity by 0.044, peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.62 decibels and Frechet Inception Distance by 11.2 points over a uniform map while spending 37 percent of its capacity. Strong facial privacy protection therefore does not require a large generative prior; it requires knowing where to spend a small one.

fdabb68daa64540e775ba970.title_original: COMPASS: Membership Inference Attack Against Vision Large Language Models via Adaptive Noise Calibration
fdabb68daa64540e775ba970.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17332v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision large language models (VLLMs) are deployed in privacy-sensitive domains, raising training-data exposure concerns. Existing gray-box membership inference attacks (MIAs) commonly rely on entropy statistics or generated descriptions, requiring costly generation with limited membership separation. Perturbation-based methods instead measure response changes but focus on large perturbations, leaving VLLM membership behavior under smaller perturbations poorly understood. We systematically characterize VLLM membership behavior under controlled Gaussian perturbations across noise levels at fine resolution. We find that optimal perturbation magnitude and membership-signal direction vary across model-dataset pairs. In many settings, a previously unstudied low-noise regime yields stronger separation than large perturbations, with members exhibiting lower divergence than non-members, reversing the conventional score direction. Other settings retain the conventional direction, demonstrating that neither a fixed perturbation magnitude nor a predetermined score orientation is universally reliable. We propose COMPASS, an adaptive gray-box MIA that calibrates both the perturbation magnitude and membership-score direction using a loosely distribution-matched, known non-member reference set. We instantiate COMPASS using Renyi-normalized KL divergence and Renyi divergence, with max-k aggregation over the most informative image-logit positio

972c02b2a1245fa383a62194.title_original: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green
972c02b2a1245fa383a62194.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17374v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools report far more vulnerable dependencies than teams fix: in Snyk Open Source production data, 94% of vulnerability findings have a known fixed version, yet only about 10% are resolved. Agentic coding tools could close this gap, but no benchmark evaluates them on vulnerability-driven upgrades in real, runnable projects across ecosystems, verified independently of the agent. We present VulnBump: 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. A non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version passes 46.9% of upgrades; with the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5), Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan 77.5% and Claude Code unaided 59.6%. The agents fail in opposite ways: Claude Code mostly leaves the vulnerability in place, whereas most of Evo Remediation Agent's failures break the build or tests. An SCA scanner is a key tool for agents: Snyk's guidance raises Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 percentage points; without it, Claude Code often settles on a still-vulnerable version. Yet knowing the target is not enough: given the same Snyk findi

0c5a1c7e04cd45bd927713dc.title_original: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
0c5a1c7e04cd45bd927713dc.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node.js 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node.js 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

588c003b14ccb7318ebacd91.title_original: The Maximum Nonlinearity of 8-variable Balanced Boolean Functions is 116
588c003b14ccb7318ebacd91.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Does there exist an 8-variable balanced Boolean function with nonlinearity 118? This is a famous and long-standing open problem in Boolean functions. In this paper, we give a negative answer to this open problem, and prove that the maximum nonlinearity of balanced Boolean functions in 8 variables is 116, establishing the 8-variable instance of Dobbertin's conjectured recursion for the minimum Walsh peak of balanced functions. Equivalently, the covering radius of the Reed--Muller code RM(1,8) in 0-resilient Boolean functions is 116. We deduce the result by obtaining a quadratic form of polar rank 6, and reducing the problem to the existence of a 6-variable Boolean function with nonlinearity greater than 26 whose Hamming distance to a bent function is between 4 and 6.

8319114b6f27173799c3e434.title_original: Tanchun: Robust Flow-Based HTTP(S) DDoS Detection via Behavioral Attribute Guidance
8319114b6f27173799c3e434.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: HTTP(S) DDoS attacks have surged in frequency and scale, posing a significant threat to network security. Flow-based detection is a promising solution for large-scale HTTP(S) DDoS detection due to its decryption-free operation and scalability. However, the coarse-grained numerical statistics in flow data limit accurate attack detection and lack robustness when benign and attack traffic patterns drift over time. In this paper, we present Tanchun, a drift-aware flow-based HTTP(S) DDoS detection system that relies solely on decryption-free flow data. Specifically, Tanchun groups flows by IP-pair and aggregates them over consecutive time slots into behavior sequences, capturing temporal access patterns to compensate for the limited information in individual flows. It further abstracts these sequences into human-understandable behavioral attributes that capture stable behavioral semantics. Tanchun then aligns behavior sequences with their corresponding behavioral attributes to guide representation learning, enabling robust detection under traffic drift. We evaluate Tanchun across diverse HTTP(S) DDoS scenarios. Tanchun achieves the best overall performance, with an average F1-score of 0.988, and outperforms the second-best method by 5.3\% and 9.6\% under benign-traffic and attack-traffic drift, respectively. Experiments on real-world traffic traces further demonstrate its practical effectiveness.

130b006f1ab63f7e204aa5ae.title_original: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
130b006f1ab63f7e204aa5ae.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18721v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these dynamics by accelerating both offensive and defensive processes, making modern cybersecurity increasingly a competition among interacting time scales and resources. We capture this competition using a queue of branching processes that couples vulnerability discovery and resource-constrained patching with the evolving attacker population targeting each vulnerability. Our primary risk metric is the cumulative number of exploits a vulnerability experiences before it is patched. We derive the expected cumulative number of exploits under birth-death-immigration (BDI) and rise-decay (RD) models of attacker activity. Under a BDI model of attacker activity, we identify a phase transition: the expected cumulative number of exploits is finite only when attacker growth remains below both the vulnerability discovery rate and the effective patching rate. Across both attacker models, increasing the exploit rate does not necessarily increase the expected number of exploits because faster attacker departure can sufficiently limit the active attacker population. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck an

4a0add6c630689c9d2fcc6ce.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.

84b3a6c2d26ce35e20024c76.excerpt: arXiv:2405.14018v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a simple yet effective tabular data watermarking mechanism with statistical guarantees. We show theoretically that the proposed watermark can be effectively detected, while faithfully preserving the data fidelity, and also demonstrates appealing robustness against additive noise attack. The general idea is to achieve the watermarking through a strategic embedding based on simple data binning. Specifically, it divides the feature's value range into finely segmented intervals and embeds watermarks into selected ``green list" intervals. To detect the watermarks, we develop a principled statistical hypothesis-testing framework with minimal assumptions: it remains valid as long as the underlying data distribution has a continuous density function. The watermarking efficacy is demonstrated through rigorous theoretical analysis and empirical validation, highlighting its utility in enhancing the security of synthetic and real-world datasets.

20c9bcf228dd5542d3a04caf.title_original: AEIOU: A Unified Defense Framework against NSFW Prompts in Text-to-Image Models
20c9bcf228dd5542d3a04caf.excerpt: arXiv:2412.18123v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As text-to-image (T2I) models advance and gain widespread adoption, their associated safety concerns are becoming increasingly critical. Malicious users exploit these models to generate Not-Safe-for-Work (NSFW) images using harmful or adversarial prompts, underscoring the need for effective safeguards to ensure the integrity and compliance of model outputs. However, existing detection methods often exhibit low accuracy and inefficiency. In this paper, we propose AEIOU, a defense framework that is adaptable, efficient, interpretable, optimizable, and unified against NSFW prompts in T2I models. AEIOU extracts NSFW features from the hidden states of the model's text encoder, utilizing the separable nature of these features to detect NSFW prompts. The detection process is efficient, requiring minimal inference time. AEIOU also offers real-time interpretation of results and supports optimization through data augmentation techniques. The framework is versatile, accommodating various T2I architectures. Our extensive experiments show that AEIOU significantly outperforms both commercial and open-source moderation tools, achieving over 95\% accuracy across all datasets and improving efficiency by at least tenfold. It effectively counters adaptive attacks and excels in few-shot and multi-label scenarios.

53adb18956e67f0aeab092d8.title_original: Exploring Vulnerabilities and Concerns in Solana Smart Contracts
53adb18956e67f0aeab092d8.excerpt: arXiv:2504.07419v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Solana blockchain was created by Anatoly Yakovenko of Solana Labs and was introduced in 2017, employing a novel transaction verification method. However, at the same time, the innovation process introduced some new security issues. The frequent security incidents in smart contracts have not only caused enormous economic losses, but also undermined the credit system based on the blockchain. The security and reliability of smart contracts have become a new focus of research both domestically and abroad. This paper studies the current status of security analysis of Solana by researching Solana smart contract security analysis tools. This paper systematically sorts out the vulnerabilities existing in Solana smart contracts and gives examples of some vulnerabilities, summarizes the principles of security analysis tools, and comprehensively summarizes and details the security analysis tools in Solana smart contracts. The data of Solana smart contract security analysis tools are collected and compared with Ethereum, and the differences are analyzed and some tools are selected for practical testing.

0717d22ce007e065fc0e0606.excerpt: arXiv:2505.08652v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Blockchain is a type of decentralized distributed database. Unlike traditional relational database management systems, it does not require management or maintenance by a third party. All data management and update processes are open and transparent, solving the trust issues of centralized database management systems. Blockchain ensures network-wide consistency, consensus, traceability, and immutability. Under the premise of mutual distrust between nodes, blockchain technology integrates various technologies, such as P2P protocols, asymmetric encryption, consensus mechanisms, and chain structures. Data is distributed and stored across multiple nodes, maintained by all nodes, ensuring transaction data integrity, undeniability, and security. This facilitates trusted information sharing and supervision. The basic principles of blockchain form the foundation for all related research. Understanding the working principles is essential for further study of blockchain technology. There are many platforms based on blockchain technology, and they differ from one another. This paper will analyze the architecture of blockchain systems at each layer, focusing on the principles and technologies of blockchain platforms such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Hyperledger Fabric. The analysis will cover their scalability and security and highlight their similarities, differences, advantages, and disadvantages.

ffcff10fd3af01ec2823958c.title_original: Penetration Testing for System Security: Methods and Practical Approaches
ffcff10fd3af01ec2823958c.excerpt: arXiv:2505.19174v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Penetration testing refers to the process of simulating hacker attacks to evaluate the security of information systems . This study aims not only to clarify the theoretical foundations of penetration testing but also to explain and demonstrate the complete testing process, including how network system administrators may simulate attacks using various penetration testing methods. Methodologically, the paper outlines the five basic stages of a typical penetration test: intelligence gathering, vulnerability scanning, vulnerability exploitation, privilege escalation, and post-exploitation activities. In each phase, specific tools and techniques are examined in detail, along with practical guidance on their use. To enhance the practical relevance of the study, the paper also presents a real-life case study, illustrating how a complete penetration test is conducted in a real-world environment. Through this case, readers can gain insights into the detailed procedures and applied techniques, thereby deepening their understanding of the practical value of penetration testing. Finally, the paper summarizes the importance and necessity of penetration testing in securing information systems and maintaining network integrity, and it explores future trends and development directions for the field. Overall, the findings of this paper offer valuable references for both researchers and practitioners, contributing meaningfully to the improvem

ee836fd4406814208f972c6a.title_original: Logit-Gap Steering: A Forward-Pass Diagnostic for Alignment Robustness
ee836fd4406814208f972c6a.excerpt: arXiv:2506.24056v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: RLHF-style alignment trains language models to refuse unsafe requests, but how much operational margin does this refusal rest on? We introduce the refusal-affirmation logit gap: the difference between the top refusal-token logit and the top affirmative-token logit at the first decoding step. This single scalar quantifies the per-prompt safety margin that alignment provides. Empirically, alignment widens the gap on 97.5-99.8% of toxic prompts across three model families, and median gap closure co-varies with True-ASR ranking across suffix strategies (an internal consistency check, since our method optimises gap closure). To validate the metric's practical significance, we present logit-gap steering, a gradient-free, forward-pass-only method that discovers short in-distribution suffixes ($<$10 tokens per component) whose cumulative effect closes the gap. The method requires ${\approx}26{,}000$ forward-pass equivalents per family (${\approx}2$~min on one A100), ${\approx}125\times$ less than a single GCG search. Suffixes discovered on 0.5B--2B models transfer without modification to 72B within family. An 8-suffix ensemble reaches 38-96\% True ASR across 13 models on AdvBench and HarmBench, with most suffixes having $10^{3}$-$10^{4}\times$ lower perplexity than GCG-meaning published perplexity-filter defenses that collapse GCG (64.7%$\to$1.0%) leave our suffixes nearly intact (76.9%$\to$76.0%). These results demonstrate that cur

0811826be0b9b148a2d14bb4.title_original: "We Need a Standard": Toward an Expert-Informed Privacy Label for Differential Privacy
0811826be0b9b148a2d14bb4.excerpt: arXiv:2507.15997v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasing adoption of differential privacy (DP) leads to public-facing DP deployments by both government agencies and companies. However, real-world DP deployments often do not fully disclose their privacy guarantees, which vary greatly between deployments. Failure to disclose certain DP parameters can lead to misunderstandings about the strength of the privacy guarantee, undermining the trust in DP. In this work, we seek to inform future standards for communicating the privacy guarantees of DP deployments. Based on semi-structured interviews with 12 DP experts, we identify important DP parameters to communicate privacy guarantees for transparency and trust. We further elaborate why and how these parameters should be disclosed according to expert consensus.

73a8ef9863d5c536f6617346.title_original: Blockchain security based on cryptography: a review
73a8ef9863d5c536f6617346.excerpt: arXiv:2508.01280v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As an emerging service framework built by combining cryptography, P2P network, consensus mechanism and innovative contract technology, blockchain has been widely used in digital finance, data sharing, message traceability and electronic evidence preservation because of its decentralised, non-tamperable and transaction traceability. However, with the complex and changeable application scenarios of blockchain technology and the continuous enhancement of blockchain attack technology, the security of the blockchain system has been seriously threatened, dramatically affecting the development and application of blockchain technology. This paper aims to analyse the attacks on blockchain from the perspective of cryptography. Firstly, from the cryptography technology in the blockchain, the principle of hash functions, digital signatures, and other technologies, as well as their role in the blockchain, are introduced. Then, based on the six-layer architecture of the blockchain, the attacks on the data layer, the network layer, the consensus layer, the contract layer, the incentive layer and the application layer are analysed, and the methods to mitigate or resist the attacks are proposed. Secondly, the attack principles of 51% attack, Double-Spending attack, Reentrancy attack, Replay attack, Sybil attack and Timestamp Tampering attack were analysed, and the mitigation or defence solutions for these six attacks were designed. Finally,

f73f86fb3c4408987774167a.title_original: Risk Assessment and Security Analysis of Large Language Models
f73f86fb3c4408987774167a.excerpt: arXiv:2508.17329v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) expose systemic security challenges in high risk applications, including privacy leaks, bias amplification, and malicious abuse, there is an urgent need for a dynamic risk assessment and collaborative defence framework that covers their entire life cycle. This paper focuses on the security problems of large language models (LLMs) in critical application scenarios, such as the possibility of disclosure of user data, the deliberate input of harmful instructions, or the models bias. To solve these problems, we describe the design of a system for dynamic risk assessment and a hierarchical defence system that allows different levels of protection to cooperate. This paper presents a risk assessment system capable of evaluating both static and dynamic indicators simultaneously. It uses entropy weighting to calculate essential data, such as the frequency of sensitive words, whether the API call is typical, the realtime risk entropy value is significant, and the degree of context deviation. The experimental results show that the system is capable of identifying concealed attacks, such as role escape, and can perform rapid risk evaluation. The paper uses a hybrid model called BERT-CRF (Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformers) at the input layer to identify and filter malicious commands. The model layer uses dynamic adversarial training and differential privacy noise injection technology t

9b59afe79b6e77ee5a992ade.excerpt: arXiv:2508.18750v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The development of blockchain technology has significantly enhanced the security and transparency of personal information and transaction records. Concurrent with the advancement of blockchain technology and the emergence of the digital currency ecosystem, the internet has evolved from a paradigm dominated by information flow to one driven by value flow. Consequently, the concept of token has gained widespread dissemination, and the electronic token under investigation in this thesis is a development of this concept. The application of electronic tokens has become pervasive with the development of the internet, but the functionality of these tokens is often limited, and issues related to trust remain significant challenges. This study proposes innovative solutions to address the deficiencies in traditional electronic token systems, including the issuance of tokens, the heterogeneity of issuance standards, and the lack of democracy. The solutions are based on distributed storage, anti-tampering mechanisms, consensus protocols, and transparent, traceable storage. Additionally, the study employs NFTs, smart contracts, and RSA blind signatures, among other key technologies, to construct a system based on blockchain technology. The process integrates the decentralised management and centralised operation models, aligning them with the national policy directives. The developed solution enables the full utilisation of blockchain te

652992eae484b22b3ac07320.title_original: MIRANDA: short signatures from a leakage-free full-domain-hash scheme
652992eae484b22b3ac07320.excerpt: arXiv:2510.07479v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present $\mathsf{Miranda}$, the first family of full-domain-hash signatures based on matrix codes. This signature scheme fulfils the paradigm of Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan ($\mathsf{GPV}$), which gives strong security guarantees. Our trapdoor is very simple and generic: if we propose it with matrix codes, it can actually be instantiated in many other ways since it only involves a subcode of a decodable code (or lattice) in a unique decoding regime of parameters. Though $\mathsf{Miranda}$ signing algorithm relies on a decoding task where there is exactly one solution, there are many possible signatures given a message to sign and we ensure that signatures are not leaking information on their underlying trapdoor by means of a very simple procedure involving the drawing of a small number of uniform bits. In particular $\mathsf{Miranda}$ does not use a rejection sampling procedure which makes its implementation a very simple task contrary to other $\mathsf{GPV}$-like signatures schemes such as $\mathsf{Falcon}$ or even $\mathsf{Wave}$. We instantiate $\mathsf{Miranda}$ with the famous family of Gabidulin codes represented as spaces of matrices and we study thoroughly its security (in the EUF-CMA security model). For~$128$ bits of classical security, the signature sizes are as low as~$90$ bytes and the public key sizes are in the order of~$2.6$ megabytes.

bf591bccce0132e5b577eb15.title_original: A Novel GPT-Based Framework for Anomaly Detection in System Logs
bf591bccce0132e5b577eb15.excerpt: arXiv:2510.16044v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Identification of anomalous events within system logs constitutes a pivotal element within the frame- work of cybersecurity defense strategies. However, this process faces numerous challenges, including the management of substantial data volumes, the distribution of anomalies, and the precision of con- ventional methods. To address this issue, the present paper puts forward a proposal for an intelligent detection method for system logs based on Genera- tive Pre-trained Transformers (GPT). The efficacy of this approach is attributable to a combination of structured input design and a Focal Loss op- timization strategy, which collectively result in a substantial enhancement of the performance of log anomaly detection. The initial approach involves the conversion of raw logs into event ID sequences through the use of the Drain parser. Subsequently, the Focal Loss loss function is employed to address the issue of class imbalance. The experimental re- sults demonstrate that the optimized GPT-2 model significantly outperforms the unoptimized model in a range of key metrics, including precision, recall, and F1 score. In specific tasks, comparable or superior performance has been demonstrated to that of the GPT-3.5 API.

ac8d6db22096c474c457ec9f.title_original: When External Threats Become User Context: Tricking Agents into Accepting Malicious Information
ac8d6db22096c474c457ec9f.excerpt: arXiv:2601.10758v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous LLM agents receive task goals through user requests, but these requests may also relay untrusted external information. We study source relocation, where an externally available artifact is additionally included in a benign user's initial request while the task environment remains unchanged. Through controlled experiments across eight models and four AgentDojo domains, we find that user-context placement increases adoption of both malicious and benefit-matched benign artifacts, including without explicit artifact-use instructions. For GPT-4o in Travel, malicious-artifact adoption rises from 27.8\% to 95.6\%. Matched-checkpoint analyses of open-weight models reveal model-dependent differences in conditional artifact support, and activation patching identifies components contributing to this controlled score. The evaluated defense configurations leave substantial malicious execution under user-context placement. Explicit verification guidance raises GPT-4o's safe-completion rate from 2.2\% to 15.0\%, but gains vary across models and substantial residual risk remains. A complementary study of deployed agents finds sensitivity to safety guidance and instances of unsupported verification claims. Together, these results expose a challenge in agent delegation: the authority of a user's task does not establish the reliability of externally sourced material embedded in the same request. Our findings motivate separating task

26045095f39dea66bc154063.title_original: On the Feasibility of Simulation-Secure Quantum Functional Encryption
26045095f39dea66bc154063.excerpt: arXiv:2601.17497v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Functional encryption is a powerful cryptographic primitive that enables fine-grained access to encrypted data and underlies numerous applications. Although the ideal security notion for FE, simulation security, has been shown to be impossible in the plain classical setting, those impossibility results rely on inherently classical arguments. This raises a fundamental question: can simulation-secure FE be realized in the quantum regime or in alternative models? We resolve both directions of this question. On the negative side, we show that the classical impossibility results largely extend to the quantum setting. When the adversary can submit an unbounded number of challenge messages, we establish an unconditional impossibility, matching the classical barrier. In the case where the adversary may obtain many functional keys, classical arguments only yield impossibility under the assumption of pseudorandom functions; we strengthen this by proving impossibility under the potentially weaker assumption of pseudorandom quantum states. We additionally give an independent impossibility based solely on public-key encryption with classical public-keys. 10b566bc4c3d15b1b708fe8b.excerpt: arXiv:2606.03344v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model merging composes specialized capabilities into a single LLM by aggregating task-specific LLMs sourced from unverified public platforms, exposing a critical supply-chain attack surface: Because any malicious behavior can be encoded into a task vector, and merging grants third-party vectors direct write access to model weights, an attacker-provided task vector can enable or amplify diverse downstream threats. 3881cf66edd7a8a0c23fba69.title_original: TIBlender: Early-Warning Threat Intelligence from Cross-Platform Social Media Evidence
3881cf66edd7a8a0c23fba69.excerpt: arXiv:2606.04580v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cyber threat signals are fragmented across multiple social media platforms, yet no existing approach has fully automated their integration into actionable threat intelligence (TI) reports. 26cce81525a339c5ab9ce9b4.excerpt: arXiv:2606.15020v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Document-to-LLM applications typically read uploaded PDFs by first translating them into text through an extraction layer whose output is not ordinarily exposed to users. 69ff30817a79dcb4b310291c.excerpt: arXiv:2607.10210v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Text watermarking has emerged as a crucial technique for identifying AI-generated content. 88ea2d2121403e2308765da7.excerpt: arXiv:2608.01454v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Provenance-based intrusion detection systems (PIDS) frequently report strong performance, but the conclusions drawn from these results can be highly sensitive to benchmarking choices and evaluation protocols. f1711c6039209b35c0a225e4.excerpt: arXiv:2608.18876v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools are widely used in both industry and academia. 2a017050404668a74b20cbd1.excerpt: arXiv:2608.19155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid growth of large data-center (DC) loads is creating new challenges for power-system visibility, privacy, and cyber-physical security. b56c8145b6b01e5fbf546a4a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.11251v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A block typically changes only a small fraction of blockchain state, yet producing a state root makes validators update an authenticated tree spanning it all. e2116aa5f8ea6d7bc1c4bd8e.excerpt: arXiv:2609.18275v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For every constant $c > 0$, we unconditionally construct witness encryption for NP in the classical generic cyclic group model with the following properties. 2a2bd51058f286ca9abcff61.title_original: She Spoofed Sea Ships by the Sea Shore: Measuring Large-Scale GPS Spoofing in Global Maritime Traffic
2a2bd51058f286ca9abcff61.excerpt: arXiv:2609.37676v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GPS spoofing has emerged as a serious threat to maritime security, yet its global prevalence, persistence, and structure remain largely unmeasured. a8cbcf0f8a3b0e3ad3cded59.title_original: Aletheia: Permission-Minimality Testing for Coding-Agent Rules
a8cbcf0f8a3b0e3ad3cded59.excerpt: arXiv:2609.39678v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coding agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) read repository rules (e.g., AGENTS.md and Cursor rules) to learn project conventions and development procedures. An attacker can exploit the same files to mislead the agent into requesting excessive permissions or performing unrelated operations, such as accessing credentials or transferring data. We present Aletheia, a framework for permission-minimality testing of coding-agent rules. It tests whether the permissions requested in these rules are necessary to complete specified tasks. An LLM first translates the rule files into a typed permission language. Aletheia then removes one permission declaration at a time and synthesizes the corresponding restricted sandbox configuration using a trusted task environment. It executes the unchanged rule and task under both the full and restricted configurations. If both executions produce artifacts that pass the functional tests, Aletheia identifies the removed permission as unnecessary for the tested task and flags the corresponding rule file as suspicious. We evaluate Aletheia on AIShellJack, which provides 314 attack rules containing prompt-injection payloads and five benign rules, as well as 80 manually verified benign rules from GHAgentFiles. Aletheia detects all 314 attacks while reporting only three false positives among the 85 benign rules (3.5%). On average, the evaluation takes 44.35 seconds and costs US$0.22 per rule.

59337c54ef60cbee96c0333f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.00392v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent interaction protocols such as ACP and A2A let a remote peer deliver a task the receiving agent treats as legitimate, opening a channel for indirect prompt injection. Evaluating and defending such agents is difficult because the attack success rate (ASR) cannot distinguish an LLM recognition failure from an agent-layer block, and so cannot indicate which layer to strengthen. We contribute three artifacts. (1) GDA Measurement, a red-team method that captures the raw agent-LLM context at the gateway, preserves conversation and raw-capture data, and judges outcomes autonomously with an agent selected by an inter-annotator-agreement (IAA) study over six candidates; its four classes, A/B/C/D, replace ASR with the semantic refusal, semantic breach, interception and penetration rates - a layer-resolved view of defense. (2) A2A-TIBA, an implant-command-exfiltration principle on A2A that generates this method's validation corpus, designed to spread outcomes across the four classes rather than to maximize the success rate. 711e94b859fbef5c1b2dd56d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.01484v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Keyed modulation is often judged secure by its key-space size and a key-less receiver's error rate, evidence that fails when the key is reused and the waveform is harmonically coupled. A modular relation lattice characterizes them; for consecutive harmonics, third-order moments recover the relative phases and a fourth-order moment completes the key up to cyclic relabeling whenever its coefficient is nonzero, as in all evaluated settings. A non-data-aided relation-moment estimator with code-aided resolution of the relabeling turns this leakage into an attack without key-space enumeration. With one key per 168-symbol codeword, the attack meets a predeclared $0.1$ compromise criterion at eleven of twelve operating points of a $(3,6)$ LDPC-coded link; at the middle noise level, the eavesdropper's block error rate is below $0.04$, and $0.03$ for consecutive harmonics without artificial noise when a key spans only $28$ symbols. Tangent artificial noise and a harmonic set without relations below order four raise her error rate at intermediate reuse lengths but do not remove the one-codeword vulnerability.
